content: 1. Harmful alcohol use, diabetes mellitus, and mid-life hypertension are significant risk factors for dementia. Additionally, other modifiable risk factors specific to dementia include social isolation, low educational attainment, cognitive inactivity, and mid-life depression. 2. Reducing exposure to these modifiable risk factors at both individual and population levels, starting in childhood and continuing throughout life, can enhance the ability of individuals and communities to make healthier choices and adopt lifestyle patterns that promote overall well-being. 3. This subdomain is linked to Action Area 3 of the Global Action Plan on the Public Health Response to Dementia 2017–2025. 4. Data for the indicators mentioned are routinely collected through WHO’s Country Capacity Surveys (CCS) for monitoring the Noncommunicable Diseases Action Plan or via WHO’s Mental Health Atlas for tracking the Comprehensive Mental Health Action Plan 2013–2020. 5. Insufficient physical activity is associated with an increased risk of dementia. This is measured through self-reported data from population-based surveys and surveillance systems, represented as the percentage of the population engaging in less than 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity or less than 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity per week. 6. The prevalence of current smoking among individuals aged 15 years and above is determined through analysis of adult tobacco use surveys conducted by countries since 1990. Tobacco smoking includes cigarettes, cigars, pipes, or any other smoked tobacco products, and current smoking encompasses both daily and occasional smoking. 7. Harmful alcohol use is linked to an increased risk of dementia. Alcohol consumption is calculated as the sum of beverage-specific alcohol consumption (beer, wine, spirits, and others) in liters of pure alcohol per capita (aged 15+ years) over a calendar year, based on production, import, export, and sales data. 8. Obesity is defined as the percentage of the population with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m² or higher. Raised blood pressure is defined as systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg. 9. Dementia is a syndrome caused by brain disease, typically chronic or progressive, characterized by disturbances in memory, thinking, orientation, comprehension, calculation, learning capacity, language, and judgment. Consciousness remains intact, but cognitive impairments are often accompanied by emotional, social, or motivational deterioration. 10. Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia (BPSD) include agitation, aberrant motor behavior, anxiety, elation, irritability, depression, apathy, disinhibition, delusions, hallucinations, and changes in sleep or appetite. Management involves addressing underlying physical health issues, environmental modifications, and calming or distracting strategies. 11. Dementia diagnostic services in primary care involve assessing memory and cognitive functioning using validated tools, interviewing key informants, conducting physical examinations, and performing baseline investigations. Diagnosis may occur at primary, secondary, or tertiary care levels. 12. Disability encompasses impairments in body function or structure, activity limitations, and participation restrictions. Impairments refer to problems in body function or structure, activity limitations involve difficulties in executing tasks, and participation restrictions relate to challenges in life situations. 13. Electronic patient medical records contain all personal health information of an individual, accessible electronically by healthcare providers across the person’s lifetime, ideally reflecting their entire health history from multiple providers and settings. 14. Dementia awareness campaigns aim to educate the public about dementia, its risk factors, prevention, causes, types, early signs, symptoms, treatment options, and available support services. 15. A community-based approach integrates social and health systems to provide quality care and evidence-based interventions within the community, such as at home, in assisted-living facilities, nursing homes, hospitals, or hospices. 16. Health professionals provide preventive, curative, rehabilitative, and promotional health services based on extensive theoretical and factual knowledge in diagnosing and treating diseases and health problems. They may also conduct research and supervise other health workers. 17. A health system encompasses all activities aimed at promoting, restoring, and maintaining health, including medical and non-medical services that contribute to improved health outcomes.
